claims.claim: Pope Alexander VI's 1493 bull Inter caetera divided the New World between Spain and Portugal.
The 1494 Treaty of Tordesillas set the Spain-Portugal dividing line, placing the Falklands on the Spanish side.
Captain John Strong made the first recorded landing on the islands in 1690 and named the Falkland Sound.
Louis Antoine de Bougainville established the first permanent settlement, Port-Saint-Louis, for France in 1764.
Captain John Byron landed on Saunders Island in 1765 and claimed the archipelago for Great Britain.
France transferred Port-Saint-Louis to Spain in 1766, while Britain separately established Port Egmont.
Spain took control of Port-Saint-Louis in 1767 and renamed it Puerto Soledad.
Spanish forces expelled the British from Port Egmont in 1770, nearly triggering a war between Spain and Britain.
An Anglo-Spanish agreement in 1771 let Britain return to Port Egmont without either side relinquishing its sovereignty claim.
Britain withdrew from the islands in 1774 for economic reasons but left a plaque asserting its sovereignty claim.
Spain withdrew its garrison from Puerto Soledad in 1811 amid the Peninsular War and South American independence movements.
Colonel David Jewett claimed the islands for the United Provinces of the Río de la Plata (Argentina) in 1820.
Luis Vernet established a settlement at Puerto Luis in 1828 with both Argentine and British permission.
Buenos Aires appointed Vernet military and civil commander of the islands in 1829, and Britain formally protested.
The USS Lexington raided Puerto Luis in 1831 in retaliation for the seizure of American sealing vessels.
HMS Clio arrived in 1833; Captain James Onslow re-established British rule and the Argentine administration departed.
The 1850 Arana-Southern Treaty restored what its text called "perfect relations" between Britain and Argentina.
Argentina resumed formal sovereignty protests over the islands in 1884 after a period of silence.
UN Resolution 2065 in 1965 invited Britain and Argentina to negotiate a peaceful solution to the sovereignty dispute.
Argentina invaded the islands on April 2, 1982, and Britain recaptured them by June 14, 1982.
Argentina's 1994 constitution enshrines recovery of the islands as a "permanent and unwavering" national goal.
In a 2013 referendum, 99.8% of Falkland Islanders voted to remain a British Overseas Territory.
The UK bases its sovereignty claim on first discovery, the 1765 settlement, and continuous administration since 1833.
Argentina claims sovereignty as Spain's successor state under uti possidetis juris following its 1816 independence.
Argentina argues that Britain's 1833 return was an illegal act of force violating its territorial integrity.
The UK holds that the principle of self-determination gives the islanders the right to choose their own government.
Argentina contends self-determination does not apply because the islanders are an "implanted population" of British citizens.
The UK cites Argentina's silence on the islands in the 1850 Arana-Southern Treaty as a tacit abandonment of its claim.
The UK argues that Spain's 1811 withdrawal left the islands effectively abandoned, permitting the later British return.
Historians dispute whether the 1850 Arana-Southern Treaty legally constituted Argentine "acquiescence" to British rule.
Historians dispute whether the 1790 Nootka Sound Convention barred Britain from making future settlements in the South Atlantic.
Legal scholars dispute whether uti possidetis juris automatically transfers uninhabited colonial territory to a newly independent successor state.
Early European sightings underlying rival "first discovery" claims to the islands are poorly documented and contested by historians.
Modern disputes over the islands include oil-drilling rights in the North Falkland Basin and fishing concessions.
Regional blocs Mercosur and CELAC regularly issue statements backing Argentina's call for sovereignty negotiations over the islands.
